title: When AI Takes Notes: Court Allows Privacy Claims Against Otter.ai to Proceed

reading.body:
Otter.ai provided a transcription service that recorded meetings across Zoom, Google Meet, and Microsoft Teams. According to a class-action lawsuit, the service recorded conversations by default without obtaining consent from all participants and used these recordings to train its AI systems without informed permission. Whether these practices actually violated privacy and wiretap laws is not established; the lawsuit alleges violations but a court has only allowed claims to proceed.

The failure was in the deployment's handling of consent and transparency. The company states its privacy policy included an opt-in checkbox, but plaintiffs allege many users were unaware their conversations would be recorded and used for AI training. A human review of how users actually understood the consent mechanism before deployment, or a clear affirmative opt-in from all meeting participants before recording began, could have caught the gap between stated and actual user awareness.

It is not established whether Otter knowingly misled users or what fraction of its 25 million users were affected by this practice.

Class-action suit claims Otter AI secretly records private work conversations
Otter.ai faces class action lawsuit for unauthorized meeting recording
Enterprise note-taking apps face legal scrutiny as Otter hit with privacy suit

summary:
A federal lawsuit filed on Friday accuses Otter.ai, a Mountain View company that provides AI-powered transcription services for virtual meetings, of secretly recording private conversations without permission. The suit claims that Otter's Otter Notebook service, which works with Zoom, Google Meet, and Microsoft Teams, records meetings by default without asking all participants for consent and shares these recordings with the company to train its AI systems without informed permission. Plaintiff Justin Brewer alleges his privacy was severely violated when he discovered Otter was secretly recording a confidential conversation. The lawsuit argues that Otter's practices violate state and federal privacy and wiretap laws.

The case highlights growing privacy concerns surrounding Otter, which now has approximately 25 million users who have recorded over 1 billion meetings since the company's founding in 2016. Several high-profile incidents have raised questions about the service, including cases where sensitive business information and conversations with human rights activists were inadvertently shared through Otter's transcriptions. While Otter claims its privacy policy grants permission through an opt-in checkbox and states that data is anonymized before use in AI training, the lawsuit contends many users are unaware their conversations are being used this way. Otter says it does not share data with foreign governments or law enforcement agencies.
